author: sky.cactus
content: What is the current situation with regards to state growth?  I believe that in the upcoming hardfork there are plans to reprice state creation to be much higher, but this is just a short term stop-gap that won't scale appropriately with any gas limit changes over time.  I believe there is discussion about having state growth set at some target and then automatically adjusting state creation prices in order to hit that target?  What sort of targets are being looked at for state growth rate?

author: daniellehrner
content:
EIP-8037 limits state growth to around 120 GB / year. The increase in state creation cost is not automatic with block gas increases, but planned to increase with every block gas limit increase that we do. Like that we can keep the state growth at this limit at it will have as of  Glamsterdam

https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8037

author: sky.cactus
content: Did block gas limit increases move under control of core devs, or is it still under block producer control?

author: sky.cactus
content: I believe 8037 doesn't limit state growth, just charges more for it?  But there is nothing that actually prevents state growth from being the max possible state growth per block at those gas prices?

author: daniellehrner
content:
Gas limit increases are still controlled by block producers, so there is a risk that they increase gas limits while the 8037 cpsb (cost per state byte) value stays the same. The first versions had cpsb dynamic, but it was considered too complex and it has UX downsides, like gas estimation producing wrong results because the block gas limit increased between the tx gas estimation and the tx inclusion in a block.

It is limited by how much it can grow per year. If every block is at target and the only thing it does is creating new state as much as gas allows, it will increase the state by 120 Gb / year. It cannot be more than that.

author: sky.cactus
content: What contains it to 120GB per year, given that the gas limit can change arbitrarily (block producer control)?

author: sky.cactus
content: I'm guessing it is not worth arguing, but this EIP feels far more complex than the naive simple one which just rate limits state growth via multidimensional gas pricing.

author: daniellehrner
content: I think I know what you mean. Yes, it is assumed that block producers will not increase block gas limits without the approval of core devs. There is a risk that this changes in the future, but for the last years that worked out. And if it does change in the future and becomes an issue it can be changed to be dynamic

author: sky.cactus
content: I likely will find myself shouting into the wind again, but I don't think we should be designing systems that only work as long as the core devs can reactively fix things in the future.  We should be building systems that are robust indefinitely into the future even if the core devs all disappear tomorrow.

author: sky.cactus
content: In the case of this top, that would mean targeting a fixed state growth rate per year that is well below Moore's Law (best to minimize reliance on Moore's Law as much as we can) and design a system that can autonomously target that until the end of time.

author: draganrakita
content: This is problem for 2030, after frames, pq, binary trie and some other maintenance fork. Ethereum has around 10 years to solve this.

author: sky.cactus
content: I disagree.  State growth is, IMO, one of the biggest problems facing Ethereum today.  This is because I think that the ability for end-users to run nodes on their local hardware is more important than just about anything else.  One exception may be quantum resistance, but that one is a giant bag of unknowns so hard to weigh it against real problems we are facing today.

author: draganrakita
content: It is fine, not to agree

author: misilva73
content:
<@301186049323958275> , 8037 is a first fix that avoids the growth rate from increasing linearly with the default glamsterdam gas bump. It is true that validators can vote to further raise the gas limit, however, so far they have followed the defaults set by clients. 
As for the long term fix, it will be something like EIP-7999, where we set an average growth rate and the base fee adjusts if state grows at a higher rate. This would mean more control over the average rate without it being so directly couple with the gas limit.
We are also looking into solutions for making holding state more feasible, such as state tiering (which would allow nodes to move part of state to cheaper HDD). However, these are still early experiments.

author: sky.cactus
content: Has there been any discussion on what to set the annual growth rate to with something like 7999?

author: misilva73
content: Not yet. The current default is to just keep the current rate. But agree that we should discuss this more.

author: sky.cactus
content: I hope that when the time comes to have that discussion we decide not to keep it at "the rate that resulted in 99.99% of users not able to run their own node".  😬

author: potuz
content: In fact I think I'd disagree here. If anything block producers, while also having a perhaps biased position, are less arbitrary that letting core devs decide on state growth

author: sky.cactus
content: If I had my way, I would remove the power of gas limit changes from both block producers and core devs.  😅

author: potuz
content: We are moving into making core devs have more weight in gas limit decisions. For example we ship a default gas schedule and also default gas targets before they are decided to be raised. I think this is the wrong direction

author: sky.cactus
content: I think the broader concern is that the people deciding on gas limit changes are not the same people who are adjusting the gas pricing of state creation operations, and there is nothing in the protocol that enforces the two make changes in sync with each other.

author: sky.cactus
content: It feels like a very fragile system compared to a fully autonomous one, which we could build instead (and it sounds like is being discussed).

author: sky.cactus
content: I think both have problems (core devs pick or proposers pick), but different problems.  Proposers pick is an incentive misalignment problem.  Core devs pick means we lose our ability to react quickly to attacks (like shanghai) and core devs are far easier to coordinate/influence than the vague set of proposers.

author: ben_a_adams
content:
Looking at it differently what the core devs "need" is a cap on gaslimit (i.e. we say its not technically safe above this level); what the gaslimit *is *I'm not sure we need to force a choice, can be up to validators

Builders only choose what it is because all the validators choose to delegate their building to them, so is still the validator choice in a way (and they hint to the builders)

author: potuz
content: Builders are kinda irrelevant in this picture unless they actively censor and artificially don't fill blocks. Validators check their gas limit is respected in the builder's bids

author: potuz
content: The ultimate decision is by validators, but changing the default values, and now with a default gas schedule, it's not trivial
